item.title: An argument of Parfit's reconsidered with logical decision theory
item.description:
A logical decision theory recommends that you choose as if deciding the output of your decision algorithm.

The main difficulty in formulating a logical decision theory is how to define statements like: "If my algorithm outputs this, the result will be that". These look like counterfactual implications, but counterfactuals describe possible worlds with different contingent facts. What our decision algorithm outputs (with given input) is a logical fact, and it is not clear what it means to say what would happen if a logical fact were different. Much theoretical work has gone into elaborating this kind of counterpossible implication, without, in my opinion, satisfactory results.

But what's the point of this theoretical work? Do we really need LDT?

What's the difference between choosing the output of your decision algorithm and just making a choice? There is no difference, as long as your choice is the only thing in the world that depends on your decision algorithm. The only substantial applications of LDT are games where the player's environment contains some other implementation of the algorithm. The central example is Newcomb's problem.

But Newcomb's problem sounds like a science fiction story, and I'm not convinced by the case that analogous problems are part of our ordinary social lives.

But leaving aside the prospect of applying LDT to real life, I do think it's important in philosophy. In this post I'm going to share an example that came up when I was reading Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons. It's an argument that Parfit makes where LDT seems conspicuously missing. Like, if you were familiar with LDT, you would have gone in a different direction.

Derek Parfit's book introduces a zoo of theories of morality and rationality, which he refers to by single-letter acronyms. In the first part of the book (all I've read to be honest), he describes how these theories can be self-defeating, introducing a taxonomy of the varieties of self-defeat.

The basic principle of LDT becomes applicable when Parfit introduces "collective self-defeat". This variety of self-defeat depends on the outcome of a game in which multiple players decide according to the same theory. Because you know the other players are deriving their decisions from the same theory as you are, a philosophical move inspired by LDT yields interesting results.

Parfit's claim: S is collectively self-defeating

I'm going to use a single argument of Parfit's as an example. The subject of the argument is the self-interest theory (), which he says is a theory of rationality. (Since this is LessWrong, I must add that he doesn't mean what Yudkowsky means by "rationality", but I don't think that's important for this argument.)

What we need to know about is that it prescribes an aim, which is that your life go as well as possible, as well as what I'll call a policy: it recommends taking the actions that make your life go as well as possible, among the available alternatives.

Parfit argues that has the property of being collectively self-defeating: that is, if we all follow , then we will do worse by our -given aim than if we had all taken other actions.

(Actually, directly collectively self-defeating, but I'll skip Parfit's distinction between direct and indirect.)

Maybe being collectively self-defeating is fine—Parfit does not say it's grounds for rejecting . What's special about this argument is that it is the first argument in the book—not the most important one—where an LDT-inspired move goes somewhere interesting.

I'll begin by paraphrasing the argument, and then we'll reconsider from a perspective informed by LDT.

Parfit's argument: S in the prisoner's dilemma

The argument that is collectively self-defeating begins by considering two theorists in a prisoner's dilemma, with which I assume you are familiar.

recommends defection, since you cannot affect what your opponent does, and regardless of what they do, it is better to defect.

Therefore both players defect, and each player is worse off than they would have been if they had both cooperated.

is collectively self-defeating, since by following 's recommendation to defect, both players have done worse by their -given aim than if they had both cooperated.

Is it so clear that they both defect? Let's concede that they do. I'm going to apply the basic principle of LDT not by disputing this argument about , but by proposing a new theory, a modification of .

The self-referential self-interest theory S²

The new theory, , gives you the same aim as , but a different policy. It recommends taking the action that it would be best for you for to recommend.

I call this the self-referential self-interest theory. We could abbreviate that to . Thus the cutesy name , even though the 's don't stand for the same thing.

Let's consider a prisoner's dilemma between theorists, and assume that they have common knowledge that they are both theorists. What does recommend?

S² recommends cooperation if we assume the right counterpossibles

Assume that for each action, if recommends that action, then both players will take it. Or, if it had recommended it, then both players would have taken it. These are the counterpossible implications we need for this problem.

If we have these counterpossibles, it's straightforward to derive 's recommendation. If recommends that you defect, then both players defect. Whereas if recommends that you cooperate, then both players cooperate. This is better for you than if both players defect, so recommends that you cooperate.

Therefore the outcome is mutual cooperation, and Parfit's argument that is collectively self-defeating doesn't go through for .

Where can we get S²'s counterpossibles?

But why assume that whatever recommends, both players will do (and that if it had recommended otherwise, then both players would have done that instead)? Because the game is symmetrical: it looks the same from the perspective of each player. So both players should get the same recommendation from . And since they're both theorists, they both follow that recommendation.

We want that reasoning to go through, but it seems hard for any formal theory to work like that. I started this post by telling you that counterpossibles present theoretical difficulties, and next I'll explain how that manifests in this example.

The problematic counterpossible for S² in the prisoner's dilemma

The problematic counterpossible implication in this scenario is the statement: "if had recommended defection, then both players would have defected."

We can't do without this statement. It's why recommends cooperation.

But it's problematic because if cooperation logically follows from our assumptions about the prisoner's dilemma and , then we cannot consistently reason from the premise that recommends defection.

To see the inconsistency clearly: first, assume that you have some valid argument that recommends cooperation. Now, imagine another argument which begins with the premise that recommends defection. Insert after that premise all the steps of argument , ending with the statement that recommends cooperation. With that in conjunction with the premise, concludes that recommends defection and that it recommends cooperation. , then, is a valid argument from its premise to a contradiction.

If we cannot consistently reason from the premise that recommends defection, how can we assert what would happen in that case? Or, considering the principle of explosion, how can we avoid asserting everything: that if recommends defection then both players defect, and they cooperate, and get acceptance letters from Hogwarts?

That's why counterpossibles present more serious issues than ordinary counterfactuals. There is not just a fact but a logical argument contradicting the premise.

Conclusion

One might wonder, can you just ignore Newcomb's problem and the whole body of decision theory literature that it spawned? I think the answer is no. The kind of situations that logical decision theory is supposed to address come up naturally in the course of philosophical arguments.

When reading Reasons and Persons, the argument above was the first place in the book where, being familiar with LDT, I saw an important unexplored path that seemed to undermine the conclusion. There are more cases like that in the book, although I haven't read far enough into it to judge what that ultimately means for Parfit's main theses.

But I hope I've also communicated to you why LDT is at best a work in progress, and why some would consider it just nonsense. Theories in the LDT family include timeless decision theory and functional decision theory, and as I understand it, both of these put in the counterpossibles by hand the same way I did in this post. I won't really be satisfied with arguments like the one in this post until I can follow the logic step by step in a consistent formal theory, all the way from the assumptions about the game to the conclusion about the theory's recommendation.

item.title: R-lens: Making J-lens More Faithful on Early Layers
item.description:
TL;DR:

We introduce the R-lens: a drop-in replacement for J-lens that produces clearer readouts on earlier layers. We fit the R-lens on Jacobians computed through an LRP-modified backward pass, using the gradient-propagation rules from relevance patching (RelP) rather than standard gradients, which allows us to reduce the propagation of errors throughout the backwards pass. This method allows us to surface important intermediate variables more consistently and more saliently, reduce the frequency of semantically-irrelevant readouts, and even detect relevant concepts that J-lens misses entirely.



Introduction

Motivation:

The J-lens is a powerful tool for surfacing intermediate variables in the workspace layers of a model, but we find readouts in early layers to often be noisy and largely uninterpretable. Plausibly, either J-lens is degenerate at these depths and fails to resolve content that is in fact present, or the early residual stream genuinely carries no linearly accessible, causally relevant verbalizable content.

We suspect that this is a structural issue with J-lens. J-lens is fit by backpropagating from the final-layer residual stream down to the residual stream at the readout layer. As such, early layer readouts often fail to surface intermediates due to errors in the estimator accumulating over several layers. In this post, we ask whether we can improve on J-lens to minimize such errors and achieve cleaner, causally relevant readouts at early layers.

What is RelP and why are we using it?

Relevance Patching (RelP) is a method for efficiently approximating activation patching. It keeps the structure of attribution patching, which takes the dot product of an activation difference against a backward-pass, but swaps the local gradient for a propagation coefficient derived from Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP). This sends relevance backward under per-component rules instead of raw autograd. RelP's improvements over gradient-based attribution are concentrated in the residual stream and MLP outputs.

We therefore use LRP as a drop-in replacement inside J-lens. We fit the R-lens exactly as before but with LRP rules installed in the backward pass, so what gets transported and averaged is a relevance coefficient rather than a raw gradient. R-lens is also cheap and easy to implement, only requiring us to add a few stop gradients to the backward pass.

Background

J lens:

The Jacobian lens characterizes an activation by its first-order causal effect on the model's outputs, averaged over contexts and token positions. Concretely, it replaces every layer downstream of the readout point with a single linear map, followed by the model's own unembedding, producing a ranked list of vocabulary tokens for that activation.

LRP:

LRP assigns a relevance score to each component and propagates it backward through the model, redistributing relevance from a layer's outputs to its inputs according to rules specific to each component type. LRP preserves ‘total relevance’ from one layer to the next and constructs specialized rules to patch relevance in places where ordinary gradients would break that conservation.

In particular, we make use of four LRP rules:

  • LN-rule: treat the normalization denominator √(ε + Var[x]) as constant, making the norm linear and preventing relevance collapse.
  • Identity-rule: detach the nonlinear factor of GELU/SiLU, so the activation's backward pass becomes a per-element linear map.
  • Half-rule: split relevance evenly across a multiplicative gate's two branches instead of double-counting through the product.
  • 0-rule: for linear layers, LRP is just Gradient×Input which is what autograd does as well so nothing changes here.

Method: the R-Lens

Dense models:

  • What we modify
    • LN-rule on the residual-stream RMSNorms: replace the forward with a copy that detached the normalization factor
    • Identity rule + half-rule on the gated MLP: The identity-rule makes SiLU backward a per-element linear map (gradient is just sigmoid(z) instead of the full SiLU derivative), and the half-rule splits relevance evenly between the gate path and the up path instead of double-counting through the bilinear product
  • What we do not modify:
    • All linear layers (the LRP 0-rule produces the same thing as autograd’s ordinary gradient)
    • Attention
    • q/k norms

MoE models:

  • We use a similar setup to dense models, with a few modifications to account for the architectural differences:
    • We extend the LRP rules to all routed experts (i.e. we treat all experts as if they were normal MLP layers)
    • We freeze the expert routing weights (+softmax/sigmoid scoring, router logits, and gate projection)
    • We multiply the shared expert’s output by a constant and sweep over a few values of the constant, which amplifies the shared expert’s importance
    • Note: DeepSeek-v4-flash’s residual stream uses manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC), which means that the state carried between sublayers is a matrix $X_l \in \mathbb{R}^\{4 imes d\}.
      • For this model, we additionally freeze the mHC residual-mixing coefficients

Results

Quantitative comparisons:

Evals:

Our evals are similar in content to those described in Appendix A.6 of the J-lens paper. We probe on the bolded token position:

  • Multihop: 2-hop factual questions
    • Example:
      • Prompt: “the color of the planet fourth from the Sun is”
      • Intermediate: “Mars”
  • Multilingual: model using English representations given a non-English prompt
    • Example:
      • Prompt: “lo opuesto de ‘grande’ es” (“the opposite of ‘big’ is”)
      • Intermediate: “small”
  • Association: a short passage that evokes an unnamed concept
    • Example:
      • Prompt: “She couldn't buy groceries anymore without strangers whispering, pointing, and holding up their phones.”
      • Intermediate: “fame”
  • Typo: a passage with a common misspelled word
    • Example:
      • Prompt: “We made a reservation at our favorite resturant"
      • Intermediate: “restaurant”
  • Poetry: the first half of a rhyming couplet
    • Example:
      • Prompt: “A rhyming couplet: A wagging tail came bounding through the fog, ”
      • Intermediate: “dog”

Metrics:

  • Mean pass@10 over layers and categories (i.e. in layer x, does the intermediate appear in the top 10 J-lens readout at the target position)
  • Pass@10 per layer and per category

Results:

  • R-lens shows a substantial quantitative advantage over J-lens as models scale
    • There is no R-lens advantage for both the smallest dense and MoE models we tested (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3.5-122b-a10b). But the R-lens for every other model shows an improvement over J-lens, for both pass@10 averaged over the first half of layers and averaged over all layers.
    • This advantage increases with model size, with the biggest R-lens advantages being on the largest model sizes we tested: DeepSeek-V4-Flash (a 284B-parameter/13B-active MoE model) and the three 27B dense models (individual per-layer pass@10 plots shown for each eval category below).


Qualitative comparisons (example rollouts):

Layer at which the target concept first appears:

  • The R-lens often surfaces important intermediate concepts at earlier layers than the J-lens
  • Example: typo prompt
    • On the misspelled word “aganst”, R-lens surfaces the correctly-spelled “against” at rank 1 at layer 4, while J-lens never surfaces “against” on the token position where the typo occurs
  • Example: multihop
    • On the token “sushi”, R-lens surfaces the intermediate “Japan” at layer 2, while J-lens does not surface it until layer 14 
  • Example: basic readout
    • On the token “Jordan”, R-lens surfaces the token “basketball” at layer 4, while J-lens surfaces it at layer 20


R-lens captures early-layer concepts that J-lens never surfaces:

  • We show above that R-lens is often able to read out concepts at earlier layers than J-lens
  • But R-lens doesn’t just give us earlier readouts of the same concepts: R-lens can surface concepts that appear exclusively in earlier layers, which J-lens entirely misses
  • Example: on the token “Verona”, R-lens surfaces “Italy” at rank 1 around layer 5, while it has rank >1000 with J-lens
  • Example: in a prompt briefly mentioning Albert Einstein, the token “ physicists” is surfaced in the top 10 by R-lens around layers 6-17 but not by J-lens

Content of early layers:

  • In early layers, J-lens tends to contain what we refer to as “trash tokens”: tokens that are seemingly non-semantic, incoherent, or unrelated to the prompt
    • E.g. “锁定” ("locking"), “尷” (half of "awkward"), “＊＊＊＊＊＊＊＊”, “ ... ”, “......”, “euw”, “tav”, “zinho”, etc.
    • One possible interpretation: early layers do not contain the types of “verbalizable representations” that define workspace content, so there is in effect nothing for J-lens to surface. When we try to surface the “unverbalizable content” in the early layers with J-lens, we get these incoherent readouts.
  • However, R-lens seems to contain drastically fewer trash tokens in the early layers
    • Instead, we see the model echoing similar tokens to those that have come up earlier in the prompt
      • E.g. for the prompt below, after “color”, we see “颜色的” (“of color” in Chinese); after “fourth”, we see “fifth”
    • We even see examples of “interpretative meta-tokens” coming up on very early layers
      • E.g. for the prompt below, the token “是什么呢” (“what is this?”) pops up as early as L6 when the model is trying to do the multihop computation

Causal analysis:

  • Setup: on 30 questions from the multihop eval set, we ablate the projection of the R-lens, J-lens, and logit lens directions for the intermediate token from the activations on the penultimate token position of the prompt.
    • We test ablating only on the first half of layers (to test saliency of early representations for each method) and ablating on all layers
    • We test the relative accuracy loss (judged with a GPT 5.4 nano autorater): we sample each prompt 8 times before and after ablating, and measure the reduction in accuracy across all 30 prompts
  • Results:
    • On nearly all models (with the exception of the two smaller MoEs on the first half of layers), ablating the R-lens directions for the intermediates results in a much larger decrease in accuracy than ablating J-lens or logit lens directions.
    • This suggests that the R-lens directions for intermediates are more causally important for determining the answer, especially on the largest model, Deepseek-V4-Flash.


Training probes to find an upper bound on capabilities:

  • Setup:
    • We train linear probes to distinguish between 10 concepts within a category (e.g. for athletes, we train a linear classifier on 10 famous athletes)
    • On a simple factual recall question (e.g. “The athlete Michael Jordan plays the sport of”), we find the earliest layer where these probes get 0.99-1.00 accuracy
      • These layers represent an “upper bound” on how early we can expect lens readouts to identify concepts
  • Results:
    • We find that R-lens consistently appears at earlier layers than J-lens, getting significantly closer to the probe-defined upper bound.


CKA analysis: We found R-lens to be more different than J-lens in early layers and the R-space CKA to show roughly 2-3 distinct bands as opposed to J-space CKA’s 4-5 for Qwen-3.6-27b.

Acknowledgements

This work was supported by the MATS program.

Appendix

Do MLP layers preferentially amplify RelP lens directions?

We measure the MLP gain (how strongly the information encoded by a direction v is amplified by the next MLP block) of directions from J-lens, R-lens, and logit lens compared to those of a standard MLP neuron. This is similar to the experiment from Figure 32 of the J-lens paper. We find that on Qwen3.6-27B, J-lens and R-lens directions are similarly amplified across layers, and these are significantly more amplified than the MLP neuron in later workspace layers.


Quantitative eval results for smaller models

item.title: An International AI Slowdown Is Ready Whenever Politicians Are
item.description:
Linkpost for a piece we recently published for AI Frontiers in the wake of recent calls for slowdown, covering how an international verification effort be trivially enforced by using human inspectors alone and the joint incentives for implementing one.

On July 28, over a thousand employees of the world’s top AI companies advocated that the US government “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” Following months of cybersecurity scares and their own loss of control incidents, both OpenAI and Anthropic officially endorsed the same message, recognizing the danger of blindly accelerating AI development.

Despite this new urgency, many people argue that coordinating an international slowdown is currently unworkable—including some of the same groups in favor of one. Namely, they claim that even if the US slowed down its own AI development, it wouldn’t be able to make sure that China was doing the same, leaving the US no choice but to race.

These anti-slowdown arguments usually emphasize the technical challenges with designing AI monitoring measures to ensure a slowdown is being respected. In particular, slowdown skeptics argue that countries would refuse to install verification measures unless they were privacy-preserving enough to avoid leaking trade secrets and other sensitive information. They then point out that any near-term privacy-preserving verification technology would not be adversarially robust to nation-state attacks. If the Chinese government were actively trying to subvert a slowdown, it could use advanced techniques to fake workloads and spoof locations, including physical key extraction or even laser bit-flipping. Getting to the point where we can start implementing an international slowdown, the argument goes, might have to wait on years of R&D to solve both these problems.

This perspective is missing the forest for the trees. Privacy-preserving verification tools that are immune to state adversaries would be ideal, but they are not a prerequisite for an AI slowdown. Robustly verifying limits on AI development is already feasible with low-tech methods. If there were enough political will to implement a joint slowdown, states could extensively monitor labs for unsanctioned behavior by simply placing human inspectors on the inside—an approach we call Whole-Lab Inspection (WLI).

Under this proposal, inspectors from the US and China would receive broad physical access to frontier AI companies alongside read-only access to corporate communications, worklogs, code repositories, and compute telemetry. Using monitoring systems the companies already operate, they could observe operations and investigate potential violations—giving them the visibility of a CISO without requiring the powers of an operator. By literally and figuratively looking over the shoulders of lab employees, inspectors would likely be capable of robustly verifying fine-grained restrictions on AI development, such as bans on autonomous AI R&D and limitations on post-training. Overall, WLI demonstrates that an international slowdown is already technically possible; it’s just a question of whether the US and China will have the political will to jointly implement it.

In the near future, political will to implement a joint slowdown could rapidly appear. If developed and diffused quickly, advanced AI systems are likely to intensely destabilize society by democratizing access to weapons of mass destruction and fueling waves of unemployment, regardless of whether they’re developed at home or abroad. On top of these threats, allowing an intelligence explosion would risk military escalation and loss of control, as states race to sabotage and deploy powerful AI systems for strategic advantage. Should the US slow down its own AI development domestically in anticipation of this instability and offer a reciprocal audit, China would have strong incentives to agree—both to ensure the U.S. does not recklessly deploy its own AI systems, and to avoid the chance of spiraling escalation over AI development.

In what follows, we’ll argue that whole-lab inspections can be used to robustly enforce fine-grained limits on AI development. Then, we’ll speak to the incentives that might encourage the US and China to pursue a joint slowdown at some point using WLI. Finally, we’ll discuss the stability and risk reduction benefits of a well-timed slowdown.

Enforcing a Slowdown Through Whole-Lab Inspections

In order to agree to a slowdown, the US and China would need to know what research was being conducted inside each other’s frontier labs. Fortunately, visibility into AI development could be achieved by sending human auditors to comprehensively monitor labs.

Auditors can have high visibility into AI companies. Monitoring for disallowed training runs or prohibited research activities may be largely trivial with human inspectors. In large part, this is because AI companies already have extensive internal monitoring systems. Most AI companies record employee screens and keystrokes to produce training data and help with automation. Companies also constantly save logs from experiments and jobs submitted to keep track of compute use and archive research progress. Giving inspectors comprehensive visibility into a lab is likely as simple as integrating and handing over read-only permissions to internal logs and company communications. To aid in their oversight, inspectors might direct a company’s own AI agents, or trusted external AIs, to read through troves of company data in search of potential violations for further review.

Alongside this digital information, inspectors could also work on-site alongside lab and datacenter employees, giving them physical access to hardware and research projects. Just as for nuclear power plants, banks, or any other high-risk industry, inspectors would be able to question employees about their work, as well as physically inspect infrastructure by hand for compliance. By using such a broad set of simple verification techniques, it would be extremely difficult to conduct an unapproved training run unnoticed—like trying to get a plane off a runway without getting noticed by an air-traffic controller.

If whole lab inspection were established, governments could then enforce a wide range of policies to slow AI development:

Preventing an intelligence explosion. The most dangerous path for AI development to take would be a full-throttle intelligence explosion—using AIs to autonomously design new, even smarter AI systems recursively. Since AIs can work much faster than humans, and since this process might quickly result in AI systems more capable than their human monitors, it’s likely that it would become impossible for humans to effectively oversee their AIs or intervene if they misbehave. To prevent this, inspectors could enforce targeted interventions designed to specifically restrict autonomous AI R&D, such as by triaging the jobs that are using the most compute and auditing whether they’re being used for capabilities research. On top of these restrictions, inspectors could limit the length of time that agents are allowed to work autonomously, monitor the amount of compute allocated to internal inference, and prevent AIs from taking high-stakes actions like starting training runs or authorizing new deployments.

Limits on post-training. Given the wide range of potential risks from AI, governments might also want to expand training restrictions beyond just interventions against autonomous AI R&D. One natural way to do this would be to place limits on post-training. By measuring the increase in capability and efficiency of a model after post-training, inspectors would have clear criteria to disallow the deployment of a model or the kinds of training environments that produced it. Likewise, inspectors could monitor which broad capabilities post-training datasets are targeting—such as coding, computer use, or medical diagnosis—and (dis)allow them on that basis. Since auditors would be able to directly observe which capabilities post-training datasets target and affect, this would allow them to cleanly whitelist certain types of post-training, even in a slowdown. These could include direct safety training to improve AIs’ adversarial robustness or propensity not to misbehave, as well as narrow AI-for-science efforts aimed at prosocial domains like medicine and formally verified code.

Even outside of these interventions, whole-lab inspection would still allow for a variety of potential regulations. Human auditors could be used to ensure, for instance, that specific datacenters are retrofitted to be inference-only, and thus incapable of pre-training, or that kill switches can quickly shut down AIs. On its own, joint verification of this kind could be sufficient for many years of delay, during which the US and China would have ample time to develop more thorough and technically sophisticated verification measures.

Joint Verification

Whole-lab inspection is straightforward and effective. If prompted by a domestic political shock, it’s likely it could be rapidly implemented and enforced at home, making it extremely difficult for any company under inspection to conduct unauthorized training runs. In order to extend this initiative internationally, however, the US and China would need to implement joint verification: granting inspectors on-site access to each state’s frontier labs.

Thankfully, this agreement would not need to rely on goodwill or trust. Because advanced AI could be globally destabilizing regardless of where it’s developed, it’s in each country’s self-interest to ensure the other is not proceeding recklessly with development. Moreover, if either country refuses to accept joint inspection, they would likely struggle to hide their AI projects and insulate them from theft or sabotage.

The US and China may experience simultaneous political pressure to slow down. Many of the most pressing risks from advanced AI are symmetric. The development and diffusion of AIs that cause mass unemployment, enable terrorists, or wreak havoc as rogue agents would cause global turmoil regardless of which country created them. Similarly, the fear of military dominance could provoke a risky and wasteful security dilemma, in which retaliatory sabotage spirals into broader conflict. Therefore, in order to maintain security and stability, the US and China need to ensure that the other is not deploying their own AI systems recklessly—something they would have no way of assuring in an all-out race.

AI companies’ trade secrets are easy for states to steal. Under mutual whole-lab inspection, auditors would have wide access to data about AI development at opposing AI companies, but this wouldn’t represent much of a change from the status quo. Today, information about model development flows freely between and within frontier labs, as employees constantly churn through roles, publish research, and put breakthroughs on the company Slack. Even once these obvious holes are sealed, state-proofing AI development against theft would remain enormously difficult. Human insiders—especially Chinese nationals at US frontier labs—could be bribed or coerced into espionage. AI development is also inherently vulnerable to cyberattacks, with anything from exploits in networking software to smuggling in spyware through the hardware supply chain offering an opportunity to steal research and models. As a result of these weaknesses, any country that tries to go full-throttle on development would likely quickly find its secrets sieving out of its frontier labs, pulling up its rival to algorithmic parity regardless.

Compute tracking would make it difficult to hide AI projects. The remaining priority would be to ensure that there are no large AI projects hidden from inspectors. Fortunately, the AI supply chain is so concentrated, and chip production so prohibitive to hide, that auditing the major semiconductor and chip suppliers would let the US and China confidently measure the number of chips that exist. In practice, monitoring large datacenters could be as straightforward as forcing the leading chip producers to hand over a detailed record of their production and sales, comparing against the declared compute from the visible projects, and then analyzing satellite imagery and electricity usage as an additional precaution.

Given the factors above, a global whole lab inspection initiative could be mutually compatible, low cost, and high confidence—as long as inspectors are given physical access to frontier labs and datacenters. Even if the US or China refuses or later revokes that access, however, AI development could still be slowed unilaterally through deterrence. The global chip supply chain is the most fragile and specialized industry in the entire world: if either country wanted to, they could apply massive friction through export controls or sabotage of key suppliers. Likewise, countries could disrupt AI training through subtle cyberattacks on training runs, such as by poisoning data to insert malicious backdoors or Stuxnet-style attacks on GPUs.

Benefits of Slowdown

Ultimately, the point of a slowdown would be to help society adapt to the risks that rapid development and diffusion of AI would introduce. So far, these risks have been mild enough, and introduced slowly enough, that the government and private industry have been able to reactively address them. By slowing the improvement in general AI capabilities, governments can ensure both that society is able to continue reacting to new risks and that sufficient investments in risk mitigation are made.

A slowdown would provide time for society to adapt to advanced AI. If threats from advanced AI appear too quickly—like the introduction of new weapons of mass destruction, or a sudden military confrontation over AI development—governments will not have time to assess and reactively regulate them, forcing them to rely on emergency measures. By proactively slowing down AI development, policymakers, as well as the rest of society, would be able to react to what would have otherwise been seismic shocks. Politically, voters and Congress would be able to decide how the benefits of AI will be distributed, and the degree of transparency AI developers owe the public. Internationally, states would be able to prepare for the introduction of powerful new military technologies before they arrive and invest in more robust verification measures.

In this sense, a mild amount of government intervention early on would avoid the need for massive overreach later, keeping the pace of AI development at a level society can react to.

The time bought by a slowdown could be used to invest directly in risk mitigation. Without the intense pressure to race and increase general capabilities, investment could instead be diverted into ensuring that AI systems are controllable and that they are developed for prosocial causes. Key open problems in AI safety, for example, include the lack of robust solutions to jailbreaking or the propensity for reinforcement learning to encourage models to go rogue—issues that will likely produce disastrous results if unresolved when models are more capable. By scaling up training in domains like adversarial robustness and behavioral propensity, AI developers could spend huge amounts of compute driving down jailbreak susceptibility and attempts to escape. Other safety measures could include aggressively sandboxing AI systems, such as with fully airgapped training setups, or preserving and expanding practical interpretability tools.

An AI Slowdown Does Not Require New Technology

Slowing down AI development doesn’t need to wait on any breakthroughs. On the technical level, whole-lab inspections could be a robust and flexible way to monitor whether frontier labs are complying with restrictions on the most dangerous kinds of development. Human auditors, reading through worklogs and standing on the floor next to the people recording them, could verify nuanced restrictions on autonomous AI R&D and post-training without needing any new inventions.

From there, a global slowdown is just a question of political will—one which has been convincingly answered before. By the end of the 1980s, having stared into the abyss during the peak of the nuclear arms race, even the US and Soviet Union could recognize the need for mutual disarmament. For more than two decades, even during years as fraught as the collapse of the Soviet Union itself, this was achieved by simply allowing Russian and American inspectors to walk into each other’s military bases and count warheads by hand.

Likewise, the US and China may soon realize that averting disaster at home will depend on verifying development abroad. If inspectors could count nuclear warheads in Siberia and North Dakota, they can certainly check worklogs in Silicon Valley and Shenzhen. We do not need better technology to verify a slowdown—only shared risks serious enough to demand one.


Special thanks to Dan Hendrycks for suggesting the premise of whole-lab inspection.

item.title: Generalized atheism rules out "inaccurate simulation"-ism.
item.description:
(Reposted from Facebook, on January 17, 2017.)

I am concerned about the number of people I've heard joking about Trump's election being evidence for the Simulation Hypothesis.

Yes, I know it's a joke. I'm still concerned.

Warning: #Essay, #LongEssay

So as not to engage in Logical Fallacy: Appeal to Consequences, before I talk about why this joke is worrying, I shall first discuss why Trump's election does not in fact mean we are living in a simulation. And neither does the Berenstein/Berenstain Bears thing, etcetera.

Because atheism generalizes.

No, I'm not about to commit the Noncentral Fallacy (aka The Worst Argument In The World) by yelling "The Simulation Hypothesis is religious!"

But once upon a decade, there was a time when lots of people believed in God. A time when atheism had to be argued, not just taken for granted. There was a time when believing in atheism made you one of those weird, loud people with arguments that only people with unusually good epistemology could follow, and other people talked about you exactly the way that the anti-LessWrong tumblrsphere now talks about LessWrong.

Today, of course, atheism is just something that everyone in your filter bubble believes. But back then atheism had to be argued, and assessing the validity of those arguments required unusually good epistemology that left a lot of the audience behind, and other people laughed at those weird atheists and their snooty yet flawed epistemology on their primitive equivalents of Tumblr.

A certain key atheistic argument is so obvious as to be boring, which is of course a good sign for its validity:

"We don't see any sign of God's presence. Therefore there is no God."

"Ah," says the theist, retreating to their motte, "that's because God doesn't usually intervene in His creation. Now go away so I can resume telling people to pray for earthquake victims."

"Okay," says the atheist, "I'll be more precise: the argument shows that there's no interventionist God. And if we're not playing motte-and-bailey then that kicks hell out of most religions. All the scriptural religions record interventions. If we're not inventing elaborate excuses, then yes a powerful and benevolent God would stop earthquakes that randomly kill lots of innocent people in developing countries."

"Maybe He wouldn't," says the theist. "Who are we to know the mind of God?"

"You can only avoid that conclusion by overcomplicating things," says the atheist. "Ask a six-year-old whether a good person with superpowers would cure malaria. The six-year-old will say yes. The six-year-old is RIGHT. Since malaria is still here, there is no good person with superpowers who can act on our Solar System; and this argument doesn't suddenly go away when somebody invokes the word 'God'." The atheist pauses, thinking. "In fact, this argument generalizes to many other hypothetical entities with desires and superpowers. If there are potatoes in the world, we can rule out the existence of a sufficiently powerful comic-book supervillain who hates potatoes. If to every appearance our world just follows simple mathematical laws, this is strong evidence against every class of superpowered being whose utility function wants anything more than It wants our universe following simple mathematical laws. If there are other places, other parts of Reality, under the dominion of superpowerful beings running around optimizing those places to meet various desires as much as possible, those places really don't look like our part of the universe! The six-year-old knows that, and the six-year-old is right."

"Ah," the theist says wisely, "but what if God wants the world to look exactly like it's following mathematical laws?"

"Well," says the atheist, "as an instrumental strategy, I can imagine that we are figments of the imagination of some superbeing who for whatever reason wants to know a more exact probability distribution about what happens in universes like this one. Say, somebody in a universe like this one has hidden a buried treasure, and the superbeing is mentally simulating many different imaginary versions of our universe to refine its guess as to where the treasure might have been hidden. In this case, to intervene inside the imagined universe would make the imaginary world unrealistic, and thereby invalidate the imagination's information-value for the real-world question the superbeing is trying to answer. This would produce a superbeing that was consistently noninterventionist with respect to its imagination of our dreamed universe; and we must also suppose that the superbeing doesn't care when imagined people die of malaria. This hypothesis is compatible with our observations. In fact it is exactly as compatible with our observations, as our universe not being imaginary. And it is no coincidence that this story consistently implies that we will also not observe any miracles in the future."

"Well, what about the election of Donald Trump?" says the theist. "It's not proof, I know, but isn't that at least some evidence that there's an interventionist God?"

"Why on Earth would it be?" says the atheist.

"Because God could have made Trump be elected," says the theist, "and therefore, worlds in which Trump is elected are more likely given the God Hypothesis."

"A person with superpowers who cares about electoral results also could have made Hillary Clinton be elected," says the atheist. "The superbeing hypothesis class can't make every outcome more probable. The probabilities still have to sum to one."

"Okay," says the theist, "but the prediction markets thought that Trump being elected was unlikely, presumably under the implicit assumption of our universe running under mathematical laws. If the universe doesn't have to follow those strict mathematical laws, if those laws can sometimes be violated, doesn't that move the extreme probability of Trump not being elected back toward the middle? Then Trump's election is more probable given the God Hypothesis than not."

The atheist throws up their hands. "What kind of interventionist superbeing cares enough to intervene to make Trump win an election, and doesn't care about a million other aspects of the world that they could be intervening on?"

"Truly the ways of Heaven are mysterious," the theist says.

"The ways of science are not mysterious," says the atheist, "and they say that we don't just get to throw up our hands and say 'the ways of the experimental apparatus are mysterious' when observation fails to accord with the obvious prediction. It's just a generic excuse to blur out all the failed predictions of the theory, and if you apply it evenhandedly, you shouldn't be using that theory to predict anything else either."

"Anyway," says the theist, "I'm asking if you agree that the God Hypothesis predicted with at least slightly greater probability that Trump would be elected."

"I'm frankly not sure of that in this case," says the atheist. "When I actually try to envision that tiny fraction of weird possibilities in which some superbeing who never intervened on any definitely visible occasion, cares enough to intervene in the US Presidential election, it's not clear to me that they favor Trump over Clinton."

"I'm not saying that God, as I understand Him, would favor Trump over Clinton," says the theist. "It's just that I, in my mortal limitation, don't have reason to believe that the ineffable God is 4 times as likely to favor Clinton over Trump. If in my own imagination God would be twice as likely to favor Clinton over Trump in his ineffable plan--that is, given that God intervened, I would have guessed 2:1 odds for Him intervening for Clinton--then to the extent one believes God might intervene in the US election, and that prediction markets have not already taken this into account, one ought to shift the market odds of 4 : 1 for Clinton : Trump towards the less extreme 2 : 1 odds of God favoring Clinton over Trump. Maybe just a little, but even so, it would be some little bit of evidence."

The atheist crosses their arms, looking skeptical. "I'm a little suspicious that you would maybe have given God stronger odds than 2 : 1 of favoring Clinton over Trump, if asked in advance. But I suppose, when I envision weird beings with superpowers intervening there and nowhere else, I don't imagine them swinging strongly for Clinton. So the point carries for me, if not for you."

"So you agree, then," the theist says, "that Trump's election was to some small degree evidence for the existence of God."

The atheist thinks. "I'm not sure that's valid reasoning," the atheist says slowly. "To get a higher predicted probability that Trump wins the election, it's not enough to hypothesize a superbeing. We have to hypothesize a superbeing that cares about Trump winning the election, but doesn't care about malaria, and doesn't care about making planets move in perfectly circular orbits instead of elliptical orbits, and so on. I'm worried that you're pulling some equivalent of seeing a coin come up heads-heads-tails and saying, 'Ah, that's evidence that a superbeing made the coin come up heads-heads-tails, because the coin would be more likely to come up HHT if a superbeing wanted it to.'"

"But we're not talking about a random-looking bitstring," says the theist. "Let's say there's some event which has as simple description, but is incredibly unlikely assuming the universe runs on physics as we know it. Like, you flip a coin 1024 times and the resulting bitstring has a SHA256 hash of exactly zero. Would you not agree that this result is much more probable given the God Hypothesis?"

"Okay," the atheist says after a moment, "I think I accept that, and in that sense, I accept that the Exists Some Rarely Interventionist Superbeing Hypothesis nudges extreme probability assignments over any simply describable outcome back toward 50-50. Now conversely, by the law of Conservation of Expected Evidence, we must say the Superbeing Hypothesis is disconfirmed to some small degree every time we see a rock fall down. After all, a superbeing could have made the rock fall upward, or hover in the air; and if that did happen you would no doubt shout 'Ah, that is more likely in worlds where there is a God!' So when it does not happen, that is a tiny little bit more evidence against an interventionist God."

"So you do concede that Trump's election is evidence for God's existence!" the theist says, smiling.

The atheist throws up their hands. "There ought to be a name for the fallacy of taking a coin that comes up heads-heads-tails, looking at just the tails coinflip, and saying, 'Aha, that's evidence for the coin being biased towards tails!' Yes! Yes if you consider just that single coinflip as an isolated event, it is from a strict Bayesian standpoint a small unit of evidence for the coin being biased tails! But when a prediction market says something has a probability of 20%, it ought to happen around one time in 5! If we're all inside the strictly realistic imagination of a superbeing who is imagining many different versions of universes like this one in order to gain more information about some real-world variable, then most of those worlds, just like the real world, look back and see a big class of events in which 20%-probable events are happening about 1 time in 5. And 4 times out of 5 they don't happen. Trump's election was not so unlikely that it outweighs every other dog not barking, every other observation of the world following strict physics. Trump's election was not the sort of thing that only ever happens in the unfettered imaginations of superbeings who don't care about strict realism. It doesn't happen only in worlds with active superpowered villains."

"But it is more likely if the God Hypothesis is true," says the theist.

The atheist sighs. "By every rule of the ordinary meanings of ordinary words, and irrespective of some technical interpretation you could make of the Bayesian import of isolated events, we do not say that Trump's election shows there is a God--at least, no more than a flipped coin coming up heads three times in a row shows there is a God."

===

No, the Simulation Hypothesis is not just the revenge of religious reasoning.

But the reasoning against interventionist supernatural deities goes through unchanged for interventionist naturalistic simulators, and I'm a little bit worried about this not being obvious.

You know how it's a bad sign when scientists leave the laboratory and suddenly forget that beliefs require evidence?

I'm worried if the anti-interventionist-superbeing argument suddenly isn't obvious, once the argument is no longer about that God thingy that nobody inside your filter bubble believes in anyway, and is instead about that cool-sounding simulation thingy.

Epicurus (or whoever) was right to deduce the absence of an interventionist benevolent God by observing suffering. Later atheists were right to further to deduce the absence of any kind of interventionist God with desires such that the world could obviously be improved further with respect to those desires. Atheists were right to look around them and see a world where, so far as they could tell, no verifiable miracle had ever occurred. Naturalistic philosophers were right to see a world where, so far as they could tell, improbable things happened around as often as they should, and no more often than that. And it was valid reasoning to conclude by induction that we shouldn't expect miracles, or disproportionately frequent improbabilities, in the future.

There are arguments against noninterventionist Gods that don't go through for noninterventionist simulators, such as "God sure sounds like an ontologically basic mental entity, and minds are made of parts", or "This does not sound like a hypothesis we would naturally trip over by starting from only the observable world and extending our generalizations from there."

But all the arguments against interventionist Gods--every way the universe does not look like there is a God running around inside it fiddling with things--that all goes through without a hitch for any other kind of interventionist being with superpowers. If there are perfectly normal interstellar aliens watching us from Jupiter, they're noninterventionist aliens; they didn't intervene on Earth and they also didn't enclose all the stars in Dyson shells. Not all of the arguments against God are arguments against the existence of naturalistic aliens; but the arguments against interventionist Gods are arguments against interventionist naturalistic aliens being here in this Solar System.

So if this is a simulation, it's a realistic simulation. And the obvious reason why that some superintelligence would be rolling a realistic simulation, is that this is a simulation meant to gain information about a lower-level universe that is very similar to this one.

In which case there will be no miracles now or ever, nor is it a coincidence that this is what the obvious hypothesis ends up saying.

As we once looked around ourselves and saw a universe that runs only on math, we should, by the same and unchanged eyes, look around and see a simulation that is perfectly faithful to the kind of universe that runs only on math.

Regardless of the absolute proportion of people in simulated universes, and people in basement universes, I think we are licensed to expect that the vast majority of simulated universes where the simulators are messing around with the simulation or filtering its conditions in weird and unrealistic ways, do not look like this seemingly untouched universe. It also seems probable that there would be a large class of simulated universes which are trying to gain information about an object of simulation, and which are therefore realistic up to the limits of realism. So whatever proportion of people like you are in simulations--whether that proportion is large or small compared to the proportion in basement universes--among the versions of you that are simulated, the vast majority of people exactly like you are in realistic simulations. These proportions are not nudged more than infinitesimally by conditioning on Donald Trump having been elected President.

Similarly, the hypothesis of a realistic simulation does not even help explain anything that still seems weird and mysterious. The Fermi Paradox is that we look around and see an empty universe with seemingly uninhabited stars and frequent planets, even though the stars are old enough for life to have evolved long before now. Well, the Realistic Simulation Hypothesis doesn't help explain the Fermi Paradox any more than it explains Trump's election. If this is a sim, it's a realistic one meant to gain information about a similar basement universe, so why would that universe have a Fermi Paradox?

It must all add up to normality in the end. And the normality that it must all add up to hasn't changed since someone thought up the Simulation Hypothesis.

item.title: Berkeley Genomics Project seeking hires (and collabs)
item.description:
The Berkeley Genomics Project is hiring. If you're hard-working, reliable, ready to learn, and highly motivated to help build the emerging sector of reprogenetics, consider applying for the role of operations lead. Other roles include research & writing, policy & lobbying, and media. Also reach out if you might like to collaborate in a smaller way, or just want to meet.

Please share this post with people who might be a great fit.

Hiring & collaboration form: https://airtable.com/app7J6q9B0tBrmQ9D/pagly64GdDtsAnL49/form

Summary

Reprogenetics means technologically enabling parents to make some genomic choices on behalf of their future children. Reprogenetics offers enormous potential benefits, both by way of alleviating suffering, disease, and death due to genetic causes, and by way of increasing intelligence and other capacities. There are major obstacles, both technical and social, to bringing this area of biotechnology to full fruition. Many of these obstacles are neglected, important, and tractable.

This situation presents an opportunity to create something of worldwide importance for humanity, approximately from the ground up, on the shoulders of and in collaboration with giants. Currently, BGP is me, plus a network of allies and contractors. I'm looking to increase the size, number, and throughput of projects that BGP takes on, by hiring one to three excellent teammates.

Our work will involve a variety of different types of projects, including a conference, technical roadmapping, expository media, active grantmaking, and other kinds of organizing and advocacy.

If you're interested, please fill out the form: https://airtable.com/app7J6q9B0tBrmQ9D/pagly64GdDtsAnL49/form

The rest of this post:

  • "Hiring" describes my hiring goals and the open roles.
  • "Why join the Berkeley Genomics Project" says more about our work and why it matters.
  • "About BGP" gives some information about BGP.

Hiring

The main role I'm hiring for is operations lead. The following subsections describe how I expect hiring to go, general criteria for what I'm looking for, and specific roles in more detail.

Hiring process

Here's how I currently intend the hiring process to go:

  • You fill out the form: https://airtable.com/app7J6q9B0tBrmQ9D/pagly64GdDtsAnL49/form
  • I may reach out to have a phone call to discuss.
  • Then we might do a work trial for a few weeks.
  • If we decide to work together for a longer period of time, we'll orient around longitudinal investment: getting you up to full capacity, including understanding the field, understanding the strategic situation, having resources to develop new directions and projects, etc.

Note that pay may not be competitive. If we prove ourselves effective, hopefully we will be able to raise more funds. My hope is to find people highly motivated by the mission. My current intention is that BGP won't pay you less than it pays me. You will be paid at least $60k / year, probably more. If you're a strong candidate and money is a major determinant, please reach out and I'll see what I can do.

If you're interested in these roles but probably can't make substantial time commitments, I'm still interested in connecting with you. We could explore possible future collaborations, small or large.

General hiring criteria

Note: If you're less established in your skills or career, but otherwise might be a good fit, definitely apply. Credentials or a track record are good to have of course, but I will seriously consider good candidates without those things.

An ideal hire:

  • Can work full-time (at least half-time is a requirement; full-time is ideal).
  • Is generally reliable, trustworthy, competent.
  • Is generally enthusiastic about the mission.
  • Can thrive in a work context that is fast-paced, multi-thread, and multi-domain.
  • Is ambitious and motivated; our goals will not be easy to achieve.
  • Is ready to learn.
  • Has a serious intention to stay in the sector for multiple years, in order to recoup start-up costs and execute important projects that take years.
  • Is in Berkeley (this is very much not a requirement; just a nice-to-have).

Role: operations lead

This is the main role I want to hire for. Note: This role requires being in the Bay Area for at least 10 days in the summer, for the conference (lead-up, event, cleanup).

In general, this role will try to take on any task that I can offload. At first I would be involved in most tasks, but in some cases may rely on you more and more over time. Crucially, I would offload "the ball" to you in many cases.

Concrete activities:

  • Lead organizer for the Reproductive Frontiers Summit. I would be heavily involved in planning, copy-writing, recruiting speakers, marketing, sponsorships, and so on; you would be responsible for coordinating volunteers, the venue, catering, badges, tickets, speaker logistics, managing finances, contractors (A/V etc.), and other operational elements. For the first year we would broadly share those responsibilities so that you learn the ropes.
  • Usual operations work:
    • Handling payments (contractors, consultants, etc.) and coordinating with our fiscal sponsor
    • Organizational setup (e.g. setting up a formal nonprofit)
    • Keeping us organized (task tracking, follow-ups)
  • Various kinds of networking, e.g. sending out cold emails (hiring searches, donor / investor searches, connecting with other organizations)
  • Various kinds of outreach (finding and coordinating with podcast guests, parents, advocacy groups, students in relevant areas, etc.)
  • A bunch of other tasks

Beyond specific tasks I assign to you, we'll work together on whatever comes up. Over time, according to interest and ability, you'd gradually learn the ropes of BGP's activities, goals, overall mission, and areas for future work. You could execute projects semi-autonomously, conceive your own projects, and maybe grow into the role of Executive Director.

Role: research, writing

You should be able to process lots of academic papers—find, read, understand, extract relevant info, summarize into a report. Background in some relevant areas is a big plus but not strictly necessary. We'll decide together what you work on depending on interest, ability, importance, and urgency. Overall goals include:

  • Roadmapping
  • Active grantmaking
  • Direct technical research
  • Technical writing
  • Expository writing

Role: policy, lobbying, industry organizing

I can't define the concrete goals and methods here very well, because I don't know much about the policy arena, but it seems very important. For example, we may want to interface with various professional orgs, trade orgs, biobank admins, public health departments, regulatory agencies, etc.; and we may want to do various organizational things, such as funding structures, trade consortia, a lobbying/advocacy organization, etc. Examples:

  • third-party validators of commercial claims about polygenic scores (PGSes)
  • making biobank data available for research
  • organizing PGS companies to fund public-goods research
  • producing reports for public health or regulatory officials

If you're an expert in this arena I'm very interested in discussing plans and potentially working with you.

Role: media

There's a lot of public communication and outreach we could do. For example, podcasts, interviews, short videos, nice expository videos, debates, Twitter engagement, etc. I don't know much about this, but if you're interested we could discuss possibilities.

Why join the Berkeley Genomics Project

A brief case for reprogenetics fieldbuilding

Beneficial and impactful

Reprogenetics—i.e. human germline genomic engineering—can enable parents to give their children genomic foundations for healthy, long, capable lives. This could potentially avoid or alleviate millions of cases of a wide variety of genetically influenced diseases.

Further, parents will be able to choose to give their children genomic foundations that increase their cognitive capabilities. To the extent that parents make such a choice, those children will be more likely on average to make large beneficial contributions to the world through insights of many kinds (scientific, technological, philosophical, social, moral, etc.). In particular, some of them might choose to work on decreasing major risks to humanity, including existential risk from AGI.

There are several potential perils of reprogenetics, but overall I believe these can be largely avoided and are greatly outweighed by the benefits to everyone. Thus, reprogenetics can be hugely impactful and beneficial.

Neglected

Many elements of reprogenetics are not neglected. There are large and active fields for statistical genetics, assisted reproductive technology, psychometrics, cell reprogramming, gene editing, reproductive biology, and so on.

However, there's no coherently organized sector of reprogenetics as such. (The closest thing that exists is some polygenic embryo screening startups.)

For that reason, there are large gaps in what humanity is working on, relative to what would constitute a healthy, fast-paced sector of reprogenetics. See "Projects that might help accelerate strong reprogenetics" and the below subsection "What BGP does" for more detail about these gaps. They include: technical roadmapping, active grantmaking, events, professional self-regulation, media, lobbying, fundraising for public-goods science, and so on.

More abstractly, there is no one who "has the ball on making reprogenetics go well". In particular, there's no one who would notice important projects that aren't happening by default in academia and industry. There's also no one to take public responsibility for addressing problems of the sector as a whole and making reprogenetics be beneficial for everyone.

Thus, important aspects of reprogenetics are extremely neglected.

Tractable

Because many aspects of the nascent sector of reprogenetics are severely neglected, there are plenty of tractable, impactful actions to take. As just one illustration, the only conference focused specifically on the full scope of advanced reprotech and reprogenetics is the Reproductive Frontiers Summit, run in 2025 and 2026 by the Berkeley Genomics Project. Many first-rate academics in relevant areas, as well as representatives of industry leaders, parents, funders, and investors, got to meet each other and learn what's going on. No one had tried to run such a conference before, as far as I know.

More generally, there are many useful things to do in the sector that are not being done by default, but could totally be done now. See the next subsection "What BGP does" for more. In particular, there may be an influx of philanthropic money that wants to help but needs opportunities. Thus, reprogenetics is tractable to accelerate and to make go well.

What BGP does

Past activities

  • Technical roadmapping.
    • This means figuring out what are the most important technical areas, and what research projects would support progress there.
    • "Methods for strong human germline engineering", "Visual roadmap to strong human germline engineering", "Chromosome identification methods".
  • Project recommendations.
    • These go to (and come from) funders, investors, and workers in the sector.
    • "Projects that might help accelerate strong reprogenetics", "Some reprogenetics-related projects you could help with".
  • Active grantmaking.
    • That is, actively nucleating projects by conceiving them, finding interested experts, and getting funding for them.
  • Events.
    • The Reproductive Frontiers Summit, held twice so far in the Bay Area. The 2026 summit had over 140 attendees, including several leaders in relevant areas of academia and industry. The average response to "How strongly would you recommend next year's Reproductive Frontiers Summit to other people?" was 8.5 (n=16).
    • Smaller events (mainly talks on genomics and reproductive technology).
  • Ethics.
    • "The principle of genomic liberty", "Genomic emancipation", "Genomic emancipation contra eugenics", "Potential perils of germline genomic engineering", "The vision of Bill Thurston".
  • Assorted networking, e.g. connecting investors with startups or funders with academics.
  • Media.
    • YouTube @BerkeleyGenomicsProject, Twitter @BerkeleyGenomic.

(Note: some activities are private and so not listed here.)

Possible future activities

  • More of the above, especially:
    • The next Reproductive Frontiers Summit in 2027.
    • More rigorous roadmapping, with more expert input. The proximal aim of this is to help effectively distribute philanthropic capital in this area.
    • More active grantmaking, for the same reason.
      • For example, I want to set up a third-party validator of claims about polygenic prediction.
      • See the project recommendations linked in the previous bullet for many more examples of projects.
    • More research on chromosome selection.
  • New areas:
    • Build dialogue bridges with various viewpoints (parents, group advocates, bioethicists, regulators, the public, etc.).
    • Make various elements of reprogenetics more legible and legitimate. (E.g. surveys, popular explainers, reviews, academic papers, open letters, position statements, FAQs, etc.)
    • Funder and investor outreach.
    • Supporting innovation-positive regulation and governance. E.g. legalizing polygenic embryo screening in various countries, enabling biobank data access for polygenic screening, allowing gene editing research (without implanting an embryo), etc.
    • Something about the talent pipeline? E.g. student seminars.
    • Things we think of later.

The working ethos of BGP

  • BGP is working to accelerate and co-create the nascent sector of reprogenetics, which may become a worldwide high-impact technology. So we will be aiming high: working hard, taking on ambitious projects, triaging to find the highest-impact projects, learning to operate in multiple domains, exploring, and so on. This will be a fast-moving work environment.
  • BGP will maintain a reasonable degree of neutrality, as much as is feasible. That is, we will maintain the actuality and the appearance of not having a substantive financial or other biasing interest in any specific company in the sector, or in industry as a whole over academia. Thus, BGP and its current employees and projects won't accept or hold the following from companies in the reprogenetics sector: sponsorships, equity, commissions, salary, contracting payments, or similar.
  • The sector of reprogenetics is for the sake of empowering future children, and empowering parents on behalf of their future children. In particular, AGI existential risk can be a background motivation, but that's not the goal of the sector. BGP won't act in pursuit of that goal at the expense of empowering future children.
  • Reprogenetics will likely be a large, complex sector, with many different elements of science, tech, policy, etc., and many different stakeholders, playing out over decades. BGP thinks on that timescale.
  • BGP is taking on a role of "organizer" for the sector. This comes with some ethical rules and responsibilities:
    • Take overall responsibility for the sector going well. While the scientists, industrialists, and legal experts will be the only ones capable of doing most of the important work, no one of them is "holding the ball". BGP intends to hold the ball on things the sector really ought to do, e.g. making sure the technology is accessible, making sure the sector self-regulates in a trustworthy way, setting up systems to avoid harm, and so on.
    • In particular, over time, many stakeholders will have criticisms and complaints about reprogenetics in general or about specific projects. BGP will take these as opportunities to understand and prevent potential problems with reprogenetics. This directly helps make the reprogenetics sector have fewer problems, and also indirectly helps fulfill the responsibility of the sector to operate corrigibly as part of society. In other words, BGP will try to pull the rope sideways as much as possible, rather than getting in a tug of war.
    • Communicate with respect, empathy, and openness, even with people who are hostile to the sector of reprogenetics. Because there are many different concerns about reprogenetics, as well as social pressures, people may be hostile without understanding why they are hostile and without knowing how to communicate well or update their opinions. So one of BGP's responsibilities is to take on some of the burden of processing those concerns and social forces.
    • Communicate with an appropriate level of humility. Genetics, stem cell biology, reproduction, personal reproductive choices, and the social impacts of technology are complicated. BGP aims to develop, present, explain, and argue for the strong cases in favor of reprogenetics—but only as part of a global epistemic process that trends toward the good and the true. When you don't know something, don't act like you do know it. This way we don't have to issue corrections later, and people can rely on what we say, including the surprising and important statements.
  • BGP intends to make good use of LLM AI tools to make operations easier, to run initial literature searches, and so on. However, BGP will not use LLM AI tools to replace human reading, writing, analysis, or judgement, because that would result in poor quality and unaccountable assertions.
  • BGP is opposed to "scientific racism". That is, BGP is opposed to using the science of genetics to justify racist social attitudes, government policies, or other actions.
  • BGP is opposed to eugenics. That is, BGP is opposed to population-level goals about the gene pool, racist genetic criteria, coercion about reproductive or reprogenetic choices, and non-pluralistic attitudes about "good and bad traits/genes". (See "Genomic emancipation contra eugenics".)

About BGP

I'm BGP's only full-time person. Rachel Wallis runs smaller events as a volunteer.

We're funded by donations and small grants. Funding is not necessarily stable. I'm currently fundraising.

At the moment, BGP is a fiscally sponsored project. We may soon rebrand and then get set up as a 501(c)(3). At first, hires would technically be a contractor, as I am.

item.title: Charles Goodhart Elementary School
item.description:
I heard a story (second- or third-hand, which surely lost or gained some details on the telephone path from reality to this telling if it even happened at all) about a boy, age 7 or so, who goes to a very highly-acclaimed school. A piece of recurring homework they give the kids is to read for twenty minutes from a chapter book, and then write a "reflection sentence" about what they read, to be checked off by the teacher.

One day, new stepmom is looking over the kid's work, and notices something off: the kid's reflection sentences don't seem to be a plausible reflection on what was read. Suspiciously many of them just describe a character's isolated action with no context, or refer to story events in the first person, or start with "Once upon a time."

Turns out, the kid was just copying the first sentence verbatim out of a book chapter, and turning that in as his reflection sentence. Stepmom tries to explain that this is clearly not the intent of the exercise.

The kid isn't having it. The teacher always gave him a checkmark, therefore his way of doing reflection sentences was correct.

Stepmom is concerned, asks the kid to read to her, and it's very clear that the kid is just not prepared to read at the level of the books he's attempting. Stepmom suggests some easier books that might be more his speed. The kid refuses; the teacher said they were supposed to read a chapter book.

Another thing they do at this, again, very highly-acclaimed school, is they give the kids arithmetic exercises at the afterschool program. At this point, stepmom is pretty skeptical of the competence of the grown-ups at this school, so she looks over the kid's papers from that. She sees an error in one problem that was marked correct, and points it out to the kid.

Kid has a complete meltdown. "No, no!" he screams. The afterschool grader had marked the problem correct, so it had to be correct. Why was stepmom lying to him about how numbers work? Stepmom tries to explain that the grader must have made a mistake. It happens, sometimes.

The kid isn't having it. Kid and stepmom take the problem to the father. Dad agrees with stepmom. The kid is still crying. "No!"

Stepmom shows the kid how to punch in the problem to the calculator app on the kid's tablet—to the calculator app on her laptop—to the LCD desk calculator that was sitting in the drawer. Same answer every time, different from the answer the grader had marked correct.

At this point, the kid has run out of energy to scream any more, or even to cry. He's just sitting there, shaking a bit, mouthing the word "No" without voice, staring glassy-eyed off into the distance, as if at some cosmic horror only he can see.

There's probably a moral here. But they're not paying me to tell you what it is exactly.
